content: The methods for determining active ingredients or physical properties, other than those validated by CIPAC or AOAC, are accepted by the JMPS on a case-by-case basis. In cases of dispute, designated referee methods should be used. Typically, methods produced by CIPAC and AOAC are considered the referee methods unless proven inferior to another method. The FAO/WHO Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR) primarily provides recommendations on acceptable daily intake (ADI), acute reference dose (ARfD), and maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides to FAO, WHO, and the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues. This contributes to food safety activities by FAO and WHO. In its 1999 report, the JMPR proposed that its evaluations of pesticide toxicology and residues should, as far as possible, follow the development of FAO/WHO specifications for that pesticide. This proposal was accepted by the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues in 2001. This process allows the JMPR to consider impurities, especially relevant ones, in its evaluations. Ideally, JMPR and JMPS evaluations should occur in the same year to ensure data comparability and minimize duplication of effort. However, FAO and WHO recognized that harmonizing JMPS and JMPR agendas would take several years. Due to the primary focus of JMPR on food safety, aligning priorities with JMPS may not always be feasible, particularly for pesticides not used in agriculture. In its 2005 report, the JMPR requested clarification of JMPS activities in hazard and risk evaluation to avoid duplication of effort. The JMPS does not evaluate risks or hazards of the active ingredient itself. Instead, it assesses toxic and non-toxic hazards to establish the relevance of impurities, assign appropriate limits for relevant impurities, and determine the equivalence of technical-grade active ingredients produced by different manufacturers or processes. The types of hazards assessed vary case by case, and the assessments only apply to the products of manufacturers named in the evaluation. The 2009 FAO Residue Manual explains the relevance of pesticide specifications for JMPR evaluations. When pesticide specifications are already published, JMPR residue evaluations specify which specifications have been established and provide the JMPS reference. Existing FAO or WHO specifications for pesticides subject to the Rotterdam Convention, or those that could become subject to it following consideration by the Interim Chemical Review Committee (ICRC), are prioritized for review and withdrawal, if appropriate, by the JMPS. Such specifications may be retained if changes in formulation or control of parameters, such as the concentration of relevant impurities, reduce risks to acceptable levels for handlers, users, or the environment. Existing FAO or WHO specifications for pesticides subject to the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) are also prioritized for review and withdrawal by the JMPS, as required. If a POP compound appears as an impurity or potential impurity in a pesticide, this is explicitly stated and considered in the evaluation. ISO common names accepted by ISO are adopted wherever possible. Standard names for insect repellents published by the International Nomenclature for Cosmetic Ingredients (INCI) are adopted where appropriate. The OECD references FAO and WHO specifications for active ingredients and formulations in its harmonized recommendations for registration. UNIDO collaborates with FAO and WHO in establishing technical specifications for active ingredients and formulations and uses or recommends these specifications in its technical assistance programs. In assessing the risks of chemicals to human health and the environment, JMPS applies the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) classification. FAO, WHO, and JMPS aim to harmonize principles and specification requirements with national and regional registration authorities as far as practicable. Normally, JMPS bases its evaluation of risks and hazards to health and the environment on detailed evaluations made by national registration authorities. This costand time-efficient approach can be replaced by a full de novo evaluation of all data if an up-to-date national registration is unavailable or if JMPS recommends this course of action for other reasons. The European Community (EC) has harmonized pesticide registration and control systems in member countries, and FAO specifications are an important feature of the authorization directives. Specification requirements for agricultural pesticides in various developing countries are also being harmonized with those of FAO. The data on which FAO and WHO specifications are based are provided by the pesticide industry. Manufacturers are strongly encouraged to submit draft specifications and supporting data to the JMPS for evaluation. WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) assesses efficacy data provided by the industry to decide further laboratory and field testing requirements before the development of formulation specifications by the JMPS. Efficacy data are not considered by the JMPS. It is the responsibility of the industry to inform FAO and/or WHO of any changes in manufacturing processes that could affect the validity of specifications, as well as any changes in the manufacturer’s name or contact address. Such changes should be evaluated by the JMPS. Failure to provide this information may lead to the withdrawal of the specification. Industry is strongly encouraged to prepare draft guideline specifications for new formulation types for consideration by the JMPS. Comments on or suggested amendments to proposed or existing guidelines may come from the industry, experts participating in the JMPS, or any other interested party. Guidelines are kept under review by the JMPS and are normally considered at open meetings but are adopted in closed meetings. Representatives of all pesticide manufacturers are strongly encouraged to participate in open meetings of the JMPS. Industry groups may be invited to provide technical experts as advisers to special consultation sessions of the JMPS to facilitate fully informed deliberation of issues. However, industry experts are not involved in preparing JMPS recommendations to FAO and WHO. FAO/WHO specifications are intended to enhance confidence in the purchase and use of pesticides, contributing to human and environmental safety, sustainable agricultural production, and improved public health. These specifications may be used by national authorities as an international point of reference but are not intended to replace national or international registration requirements. To characterize a pesticide, it is necessary to determine its composition and chemical and physical properties. Parameters critical to identity and quality are identified, and limits for these parameters are selected to form the basis of a specification. A specification should be brief but unambiguous and supported by appropriate test methods to determine whether the material conforms to the established limits. Specifications may be used as part of a contract of sale to ensure the delivery of good-quality pesticides. Where appropriate, FAO and WHO specifications should be linked to registration requirements so they can also be used in the official control of pesticides to ensure that the quality of the pesticide supplied is the same as that registered. The guidelines provided in this Manual may also be used as a framework of criteria and/or parameters for the assessment of technical or formulated pesticides for which FAO or WHO specifications either do not exist or have not yet been assessed by the JMPS as being applicable to the products of a particular manufacturer. Ultimately, competent authorities decide whether or not a particular pesticide shall be used in their country. Prior to 1999, three categories of FAO specifications (tentative, provisional, and full) were developed, differing in the CIPAC/AOAC status of the analytical methods for the active ingredient. Following a transition period (1999–2000), only full specifications were adopted using new procedures similar to those presented in this Manual. From 2002, full specifications have been adopted according to the procedures given in this Manual. Prior to the introduction of this Manual, two categories of WHO specifications (interim and full) were developed. The difference in status reflected the extent of peer review of the specifications and the extent of validation of the analytical and physical test methods required to support the specifications. From 2002, WHO has normally developed only full specifications under the new procedure. Exceptionally, where there is an urgent public health requirement and on a case-by-case basis, WHO may develop a time-limited interim specification if the validation of the methods is in progress but incomplete. Specifications developed by both organizations under the old procedures remain in force until they are reviewed. Specifications prepared according to the earlier procedures were applied to all products that were nominally similar. That is, for a defined active ingredient, the specification applied to all products containing that active ingredient, provided they were of the appropriate formulation type. However, under the “new” procedures, the FAO and WHO specifications do not apply to nominally similar products of other manufacturers, nor to those where the active ingredient is produced by other routes by the same manufacturer. The scope of these new specifications may be extended to similar products when the JMPS is satisfied that the additional products are equivalent to those which formed the basis of the reference specification. A specification published under the new procedure normally supersedes and cancels any earlier specification for the material involved. Under the new procedure, only manufacturers who have submitted a data package and specification (which have then been evaluated as acceptable) in accordance with current JMPS procedures may be included.
